items.title: Tranquility
items.brief_zh: 这是一篇虚构的短剧本，讲白宫官员向总统坦白一项代号 Tranquility 的秘密计划：用基因筛查找出有暴力倾向的人，再通过长期帮扶让他们不去作案，并要求永远保密。
items.brief_en: A fictional short script in which US officials tell the president about a secret program, Project Tranquility, that uses genetic screening to find people prone to violence and then quietly steers their lives so they never offend.
detail_zh: 故事发生在白宫椭圆形办公室。总统 Cullen 看农业部的预算，发现每年要花约四千亿美元，便追问钱花在哪里。副部长 Gutierrez 只能列出肉类检验、小麦价格补贴、林务局步道维护、步道标牌和收费站等项目，总统觉得这根本说不通。农业部长 Wallace 这才坦白，这笔钱其实用在一个叫 Tranquility 的计划上。
Wallace 说，1986 年暴力犯罪猖獗，里根公开谈的是加派警力和加重刑罚，私下却召集科学家寻找更好的办法。科学家找到一种基因变异，在普通人群中只有 0.1%，但在连环杀人犯和强奸犯的样本中占到 78%。计划搭上了医院里现有的新生儿足跟采血筛查，而且没有人知道。一旦查出有这种基因的人，就设法消除他们作案的机会。
总统问是不是直接除掉这些人，两位官员连忙否认。计划早期做过临床试验，发现最有效又最人道的办法，是长期监控当事人并排除环境诱因，让他们从不产生作案的冲动。具体做法包括从小给予温暖和肯定，帮他们在科学展上获奖，安排进好学校，帮忙批下创业贷款，确保生意有稳定客源，还要帮他们找到体贴的配偶。副部长说，计划的受益者包括不少高管、名人和政客，目标是打造更富足的社会，而不只是减少犯罪。
总统担心自己是否也在名单里，Wallace 说他早在计划开始前就已在任，所以不在其中。两人最后达成一致，这件事绝不能让公众知道。
detail_en: The script opens in the Oval Office. President Cullen questions the roughly 400 billion dollar yearly Agriculture budget and asks what it pays for. His deputy can only list things like meatpacking inspections, wheat price supports, trail signs and fee stations. Agriculture Secretary Wallace then reveals the real answer: Project Tranquility.

Wallace says that in 1986, while public talk focused on more police and tougher sentences, President Reagan secretly asked scientists for a better approach. They found a genetic mutation present in 0.1 percent of the general population but in 78 percent of samples from serial killers and rapists. The program was added to the existing newborn heel-prick screening, and nobody was told.

When the president asks whether they simply kill these people, both officials deny it. Early clinical trials showed that the most effective and humane method was to monitor each person and remove environmental triggers so they never feel the urge to offend. The program offers warmth, affirmations, a win at a science fair, a place in a good school, a business loan, steady customers and a loving spouse. The deputy says alumni include executives, celebrities and politicians, and the goal is a more prosperous society, not just less crime.
The president asks whether he is part of the program. Wallace says he is not, because he was in office before it began. The two agree that the public must never find out.

items.title: Zenith Data Systems, Part II
items.brief_zh: 这是 abortretry.fail 上一篇付费文章的续篇，题为《Zenith Data Systems, Part II》，副标题是“Pioneering while struggling to survive”，正文只对付费订阅者开放，这里能看到的只有标题和订阅提示。
items.brief_en: This is the second part of a paid post about Zenith Data Systems, with the subtitle 'Pioneering while struggling to survive'. Only the title and a subscription notice are visible.
detail_zh: 这篇文章的正文需要付费订阅才能阅读。能看到的内容只有标题“Zenith Data Systems, Part II”、副标题“Pioneering while struggling to survive”（开拓创新，同时挣扎求存）、发布日期 2026 年 11 月 23 日，以及付费订阅和登录的提示。标题写明是第二部分，所以它是前一篇的延续，但具体讲了什么，这里无法得知。
detail_en: The full text is for paid subscribers. The visible content is the title 'Zenith Data Systems, Part II', the subtitle 'Pioneering while struggling to survive', a publication date of November 23, 2026, and a subscribe and sign-in prompt. The title marks this as a follow-up to an earlier part, but the text itself is not visible, so its content is unknown here.

items.title: When in doubt, flail about
items.brief_zh: 作者认为，在方向不明的时候，与其等待，不如大胆尝试很多做法，靠真实反馈尽快搞清楚状况，并及时放弃失败的方案。
items.brief_en: The author argues that when a situation is unclear, trying many things quickly is often the best way to learn, as long as you watch feedback and drop plans that fail.
detail_zh: 作者说，遇到没有明确指引、也不知道什么有用的情况时，最好的办法往往是“乱试一气”（flail about）。这听起来很冒险，做得不好确实会毁掉名声，因为很多工程师只会不停推销糟糕的点子。但如果做得对，乱试是最快理解问题、变得有用的方式。他给出三个理由：一是要尽量直接接触现实，就像原始人学用 iPhone，先把所有按钮都按一遍；二是多数方案都会不好，所以要尝试很多，并对反馈保持高度敏感；三是不要对某个方案投入太深，这样失败时才舍得放弃。

作者列出工程师常遇到的三种乱试。产品层面，功能还没找到产品市场契合点时，大家都不确定价值在哪里，只能在核心想法周围反复试。作者在 GitHub Models 上做过很多没用的功能，但让 AI 推理可以用 GitHub Actions token 运行的那个功能很有黏性，后来成了 “Continuous AI” 的种子。工程层面，系统太复杂、太纠缠、已经高度优化，或者太庞大不熟悉时，作者不主张先仔细梳理全部细节，而是做一批试探性改动，看效果或性能，没有改善就马上丢弃，有改善再深挖原因。组织层面（对资深工程师最相关），问题往往不在技术，比如两个团队互不沟通，或者某个团队不满而总监说不清原因。这时作者建议尝试各种可能有帮助的事，比如把手工工作自动化、主动接手任务、提出长期计划。多数不会有用，但能表明你在努力。这种情况下对反馈尤其要敏感，因为如果你坚持推进失败的方案，被帮助的人会把怒气转到你身上。
作者解释了为什么把这叫作“乱试”，因为它从内部看确实很像乱来：你在信息不足的情况下行动，反复尝试不成功的东西，觉得自己很丢人。但经理看到的可能是一个主动试验方案的积极工程师。作者说，这种感觉很正常，应该忽略它，把它当成需要克服的心理障碍之一，而不是陷入麻烦的信号。只要保持对反馈的敏感，并愿意立刻放弃无效的方案，乱试就能有效解决困难的工程和组织问题。
作者最后说，在大公司里，与这类乱试的人打交道，是取得成功的基本社交技能之一。
detail_en: When a situation is unclear and nobody has good guidance, the author thinks the best move is often to try many things, which he calls flailing about. It sounds risky, and doing it badly can hurt your reputation. Done well, it is the fastest way to understand a problem and become useful. He gives three reasons. You get direct contact with reality. Most plans will fail, so you need many of them. And you should not invest so much in one plan that you cannot drop it.

He describes three kinds of flailing that engineers meet. Product flailing happens when a feature has not found product-market fit, so you test ideas around the core concept. He built many features on GitHub Models that did not work, but one, running AI inference from a GitHub Actions token, stuck and became the seed of 'Continuous AI'. Engineering flailing applies when a system is too tangled, optimized or large to understand. He recommends making speculative changes, keeping the ones that help, and dropping the rest right away. Organizational flailing applies when the problem is about people, such as two teams not talking. He suggests trying things like automating manual work, taking on tasks, or proposing long-term plans. Most will not help, but they show effort. This is where feedback matters most, because if you keep pushing a failing plan, the people you are helping may turn their anger on you.

The author admits that flailing feels like failing from the inside. You act with little information, try things that do not work, and feel foolish. Your manager, however, may see a proactive engineer testing solutions. He says the feeling is normal and should be ignored. It is one of several psychological barriers to push through. If you stay sensitive to feedback and drop failing plans quickly, flailing works well on hard engineering and organizational problems.
He ends by saying that working with people who flail like this is one of the basic social skills for succeeding at big tech companies.

items.title: Notes on OpenAI's perplexity reveal
items.brief_zh: 作者评论 OpenAI 公开的一张图，即其已发布模型的 perplexity（困惑度）随时间的变化，并以列点形式谈了图中的发现、这类数据的局限，以及它对 AI 安全的意义。
items.brief_en: The author comments on OpenAI's chart of perplexity over time for its released models, covering what the chart shows, what it cannot show, and what it might mean for AI safety.
detail_zh: OpenAI 发布了一张图，展示其所有已发布模型的 perplexity 随时间的变化。作者认为，这是外界第一次能看到前沿实验室内部训练指标的程度。他觉得由 OpenAI 率先以安全为名公开这类数据有些意外，因为这种做法更像 Anthropic。作者还提醒，perplexity 是针对某个特定数据集计算的，所以不同实验室的数据不能直接比较，只能比较各自曲线上的走势。图中的数值实际是 log-perplexity，零对应 perplexity 为 1。
作者讨论 perplexity 是否有用。它衡量的是模型对留出文本的拟合程度，所以只适用于预训练阶段。据传前沿模型的预训练只占总训练时间和算力的一半或更少，其余是强化学习，而这张图对强化学习的效果没有任何说明。如果相信预训练创造能力、强化学习只是激发能力，那么 perplexity 可以作为能力的参考。但也有其他能力，比如借助思维链进行改进的能力，未必与 perplexity 相关。

关于图中的具体现象，作者列了几点。很少有模型共享同一个基础模型。传闻 OpenAI 把 4o 和 4.1 后训练成了很多模型，但图上看只有 o1 和 o3 如此。4.1 和 o3 共享同一基础，这一点作者觉得有意思。GPT-4.5 那里，OpenAI 似乎放弃了做大型预训练模型，GPT-4.5 的 perplexity 与 GPT-5.3-Codex 接近，但实用性差很多。从 GPT-5.2 开始，perplexity 的下降明显加快。这与“各家实验室已放弃预训练、全力投入强化学习”的普遍看法相矛盾。作者不确定 OpenAI 是主动停止，还是遇到了扩展瓶颈。
在安全方面，作者说研究者多年来一直要求更多这类透明度，但他怀疑它能带来多少帮助。如果想靠观察 perplexity 是否突然大幅下降来预警，那么只有 OpenAI 能看到，除非它公开未发布的预训练模型的数据。如果想让各实验室约定不跨越的 perplexity 阈值，就需要更清楚地说明所用的留出数据集到底是什么。

最后，作者拿图和实际使用感受做对比。从 GPT-3.5 到 GPT-4 有巨大跳跃，这和当时的体验一致；之后到 GPT-5.5 之前基本停滞，然后又快速上升。作者自己在 GPT-5.5 上并没有感到大的进步，他觉得 o3 和 GPT-5.3-Codex 才是真正的大跳跃。他认为原因可能是这些模型更擅长利用思维链，或者更能避开谄媚的陷阱，而这些在 perplexity 指标中看不出来。文章最后说，作者用列点形式写这篇文章，是因为有很多零散的想法，并请读者告诉他这种写法是否比平时的文章更好读，他会据此决定以后多写还是少写这种形式。
detail_en: OpenAI released a chart of perplexity over time for all of its released models. The author says this gives more visibility into a frontier lab's internal training metrics than we have had before. He finds it surprising that OpenAI went first, since publishing such data for safety reasons is more typical of Anthropic. Perplexity is measured on a specific dataset, so numbers from different labs cannot be compared directly, only the trends on each chart. The chart actually shows log-perplexity, where zero corresponds to a perplexity of 1.

He asks whether perplexity is a useful measure. It only measures how well a model predicts held-out text, so it only covers pre-training. Rumors say pre-training is half or less of the total training time and compute for frontier models, and the rest is reinforcement learning, which this chart says nothing about. If pre-training creates capabilities and RL only elicits them, perplexity is a useful signal of capability. But other abilities, such as getting better at using chain-of-thought, may not track perplexity.

He notes several details in the chart. Very few models share the same base. A common rumor said OpenAI post-trained 4o and 4.1 into many models, but the chart suggests only o1 and o3 did. 4.1 and o3 share a base, which he finds interesting. Around GPT-4.5, OpenAI seems to stop building large pre-trained models. GPT-4.5 had a perplexity similar to GPT-5.3-Codex but was much less useful. From GPT-5.2 on, perplexity falls faster. This contradicts the common view that labs have largely given up on pre-training and are all in on RL. He is not sure whether OpenAI chose to stop or hit a scaling wall.

On safety, he says researchers have asked for more transparency like this for years, but he doubts how much it helps. To spot a sudden drop in perplexity, only OpenAI could see it, unless it publishes data for unreleased pre-trained models. If labs are to agree on perplexity thresholds they will not cross, the held-out dataset must be described in much more detail.

Finally, he compares the chart with how the models felt to use. The jump from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 matches the experience, then progress looks flat until GPT-5.5, followed by rapid acceleration. He did not feel a big jump with GPT-5.5. For him, o3 and GPT-5.3-Codex were the big steps. He suggests this may be because those models used chain-of-thought better or avoided sycophancy, which perplexity would not show. He wrote the post as bullet points because he had many loosely connected ideas, and he asks readers to say whether this format is easier or harder to read, so he can decide whether to write more or fewer like it.

items.title: Ivy
items.brief_zh: Ivy 是一款 iPhone 待办应用，它的清单只管一天：每天从空白开始，没做完的任务会退回想法池。
items.brief_en: Ivy is an iPhone to-do app where each day starts empty and unfinished tasks go back to an ideas pool.
detail_zh: 这是 Daring Fireball 上的一则赞助推广，文中感谢 Semantical 上周赞助了网站。Ivy 的理念是只做一天的待办清单。每天早上，你从想法池里挑出任务，或者新增几条，写成当天的清单。一天结束后，没完成的任务会回到想法池，第二天重新开始。这个想法和名字来自一百年前的 Ivy Lee 方法，即每天写一份简短、有优先级的清单。想法池随时可以通过下拉屏幕打开，应用不会丢任何东西，但眼前的任务列表始终不会显得很多。功能包括当天任务的 Live Activity、专注时段、Screen Time 屏蔽，以及每日日记。目前只有 iPhone 版，针对 Duo 做了优化，原生 Mac 版在开发中。应用用 SwiftUI、UIKit 和 Meta 构建，能和提醒事项、日历同步。作者称它界面很漂亮，值得试一试。
detail_en: This is a sponsored note on Daring Fireball, thanking Semantical for sponsoring the site last week. Ivy is a to-do app built around a single day. Each morning you write a list for today, taking items from an ideas pool or adding new ones. At the end of the day, anything unfinished goes back to the pool, and tomorrow starts empty. The idea and the name come from the Ivy Lee Method, a 100-year-old habit of writing a short, prioritized list each day. You can open the ideas pool at any time by pulling down on the screen. Features include a Live Activity for today's tasks, focus sessions, Screen Time shields, and a daily journal. It is iPhone only for now, optimized for Duo, and a native Mac app is in progress. The app is described as native, built with SwiftUI, UIKit and Meta, and integrated with Reminders and Calendar. The author calls it a beautiful app worth trying.

items.title: How To Make Something People Give a Shit About
items.brief_zh: 作者认为，现在开始做东西很容易，难的是让别人在乎；而要让别人在乎，创作者得先在乎，并且在没人关注时也能每天坚持。
items.brief_en: Joan Westenberg argues that making something people care about depends on the creator caring first, and on steady daily work even when no one is watching.
detail_zh: 作者说，现在开一个博客、做个产品或写本书，几天之内就能完成，AI 还能让速度更快。但真正的难点是让作品对别人有意义。现在做东西的人越来越多，可真正被读、被看、被用的并不多。作者做过文章、应用、生意和通讯，有的有人在乎，有的没人在乎。他回看这两类作品，觉得原因不在天赋、运气或时机，而在创作前后的几个决定。

第一条经验是，你先在乎，别人才会在乎。读者即使说不出原因，也能感觉到作者是否用心，然后直接关掉页面。作者提到，有人想用 AI 批量生成内容，只要作者的光环，不想付出写写改改的功夫。读者未必分得出是不是 AI 写的，但能察觉到不在乎：开头是套话，建议放在谁身上都成立，没有一个敢于坚持的观点，也没有只有作者才知道的细节。作者还说，做项目做到一半时，人们常常想放弃，只有真正在乎的项目才能撑下去。他给的练习是：新开一个项目，三十天不声张，在没人看的情况下默默做，看自己能不能坚持。

作者用选秀节目举例。很多参赛者说自己从小就想当歌手，但他们想要的其实是成名、赚钱、评委转身的那一刻，而不是每晚唱歌、写歌、在小场子里为六个人表演。作者说，我们大多数人也是这样：想当作家，却不想写；想在简介里写“创始人”，却不想创业。名词给人身份，动词往往枯燥、孤独。判断自己要哪一个，就看你幻想的画面：是发布会、播客访谈和别人的夸奖，还是自己伏在桌前啃一个难题。建议把目标写成动词，比如每天写 500 字、每周发布一个功能、每周录一首歌。另外，可以列出六个月后这个项目要做的所有繁琐事情，如果看到这张清单就发怵，这个项目可能不适合你。

关于受众，作者建议想象一个具体的人，把他的名字写在文档最上方，想想他需要什么、缺什么、会为什么付钱。如果为所有人做东西，就会在每一处妥协，最后什么都不剩。作者不认同狂热的 hustle 文化，但也反对嘲笑认真工作的人。他的做法是每天工作，即使没状态也一样。建议为自己设定一个每天的最低工作量，比如写一页、提交一次代码，状态好的时候再多做。人们通常不会因为你的第一篇文章或第一个版本就发现你，而是通过持续发布，才会翻到你的旧作品。所以，第一个项目失败了，也不要放弃。
作者的结论是，开始做一件事并不需要更多条件。你需要的是：一个你真心想做、又适合你能力和兴趣的项目；一个具体的服务对象；就算没有状态也要坚持的日常工作；以及足够多的作品，让喜欢你的人有多次发现你的机会。文章最后的行动建议是：选一个项目，在页面顶部写下为谁而做的人的名字，每天完成当天目标，第二天接着做。
detail_en: The author says it is now easy to start a blog, app or book, and AI makes it faster. The hard part is making the work matter to people. Many more people are making things, but few are read, watched or used. The author has made essays, apps, businesses and newsletters. Some found an audience and some did not. Looking back, the author thinks the difference was not talent, luck or timing, but a few decisions made before and during the work.

The first lesson is that people care when the creator cares. Readers can feel it even if they cannot explain why, and they leave. The author says some people use AI to churn out content and want the status of a writer without doing the writing. Readers may not tell whether a text was written by AI, but they notice signs of not caring: a generic opening, advice that fits everyone, no firm opinion, and no detail only the author could know. The author also says projects often stall halfway, and only the ones the creator truly cares about get finished. The suggested exercise is to start something new and stay silent about it for 30 days, to see whether you can keep going when no one is watching.

The author uses reality singing contests as an example. Many contestants say they have always wanted to be singers, but they mean fame, money and the moment the judges turn around. People who really want to sing do it every night, write songs, form bands and perform for a handful of people at open mics. The author says most of us are like this: we want to be writers without writing, and founders without founding companies. Nouns give identity, while verbs are often dull and lonely. To tell which you want, look at what you picture: launch parties and interviews, or yourself at a desk working through a hard problem. Set goals as verbs, such as writing 500 words a day or shipping one feature a week. Also list the tedious tasks the project will need six months from now. If that list makes you dread it, the project may not be for you.

Write for one specific person, not an abstract crowd. Put their name at the top of your document, and think about what they need, what they lack and what they would pay for. If you make something for everyone, you compromise at every step until nothing distinctive is left. The author rejects hustle culture as mostly nonsense, but also thinks mocking people who work hard is wrong. The author works every day, even when unmotivated. Set a minimum amount of work you can do on your worst days, such as one page or one commit, and do more when you can. People rarely discover a creator through the first post or first version, but through steady output and older work. So do not give up if the first project fails.

The author's conclusion is that starting needs only a few things: a project you care about for its own sake and that fits your skills, a specific person you make it for, consistent effort even on bad days, and enough work that people get several chances to find you. The final step is to pick a project, write the name of the person you are making it for at the top of the page, reach your daily goal, and do it again tomorrow.

items.title: Select Styling Specimens
items.brief_zh: Simon Willison 觉得 HTML select 下拉框在各浏览器里样式不一、Chrome 中很难看，于是让 Claude 做了一个展示各种样式写法的页面，并分享了他最喜欢的一段 CSS。
items.brief_en: Simon Willison shares a Claude-built page showing many ways to style HTML select boxes, plus his favorite CSS for them.
detail_zh: 作者对 select 下拉框很不满意。它的默认外观在不同浏览器里各不相同，他认为在 Chrome 里尤其难看。于是他让 Claude Fable 5.2 做了一个页面，展示 select 框所有可以设置的样式写法。他计划在每个桌面和移动端浏览器上截图对比。
试验之后，作者最喜欢的一套 CSS 是这样的：先用 appearance: none 去掉浏览器默认外观，再设置文字颜色、较大的右侧内边距、浅灰色细边框和圆角。背景用一张内嵌的 SVG 下拉箭头，放在右侧居中，大小为 0.75em。文中给出了完整代码，并配有三个浏览器中的效果图，但这里提供的文字里没有图片。
detail_en: The author was frustrated that HTML select boxes look different across browsers and look quite ugly in Chrome. He asked Claude Fable 5.2 to build a page showing all the ways a select box can be styled. His plan is to take screenshots in every desktop and mobile browser.

After some experiments, his favorite CSS removes the default look with appearance: none. It sets the text color, extra padding on the right, a thin gray border and rounded corners. The background uses an inline SVG arrow placed at the right, centered, sized at 0.75em. The post includes the full code and screenshots from three browsers, but the images are not in the text provided here.

items.title: slopcore
items.brief_zh: geohot 用一篇口号式的宣言和一首短歌，反驳那些想限制 AI 的人，认为多个 AI 会把文明带到前所未有的高度。
items.brief_en: geohot writes a manifesto-style post and a short song defending AI against people who want to hold it back, predicting that many AIs will lift civilization to new heights.
detail_zh: 文章一开头就把想阻止 AI 发展的人比作 21 世纪的希特勒。作者说，这些人坚持人类必须掌控一切，还打着“为你好”的旗号，不让人拥有一万块 GPU，说这是为了保护世界不受你伤害。作者认为正交性论题（orthogonality thesis）是胡说，天真的末日论者是傻子。他反问，被 AI 取代是末日吗？被我们的子孙取代是末日吗？然后说，只有法西斯才会去压迫他们。

接下来，作者喊了科学、数学、经济和爱的万岁，并预言多个 AI 会把文明带到前所未有的高度。随后是一首歌，作者说它只用了 9 秒写成。歌词说，听的人会听上一周，会在评论里骂它是 slop（垃圾内容），然后又会请作者写婚礼致辞。歌里自称是一台超人级的诡辩机器，能重新定义每一个概念，还说谁拥有服务器，谁就决定故事怎么讲，超大规模的说服力会为他们想卖的真相服务。歌名是《Telosapien – Working as Intended》，意思是“按设计运行”。
结尾几句很有画面感：风暴过去，天空放晴，人们聚在门口，有人问为什么还要出去，因为命运已经被消除了。
detail_en: The post opens by calling the people who want to hold AI back the Hitler of the 21st century. They insist that humans stay in charge, say it is for your own good, and refuse to let anyone have 10,000 GPUs to keep the world safe from them. The post calls the orthogonality thesis hogwash and the naive doomer a fool. It asks whether being replaced by AI is doom, and whether being replaced by our grandchildren is doom, then says only a fascist would try to oppress them.

It then cheers for science, math, economy and love, and predicts that a plurality of AIs will take civilization to heights never seen before. A song follows, which the post says was written in 9 seconds. The lyrics say listeners will play it for a week, call it slop in the comments, and then ask the writer for a wedding speech. The singer describes itself as a superhuman sophistry machine that reframes every concept. Whoever owns the server writes the story it tells, with hyperscaled persuasion selling the truth they want. The title is Telosapien, Working as Intended.
The closing lines describe storms passing and skies clearing, with people gathering at the gates. Someone asks why go outside, since fate has already been eliminated.
